  • M: Memory load and store
  • W: Write back to register file

Let the latency of an instruction be defined as the number of cycles from when this instruction is executed (i.e., completes execution) until the next instruction is executed (i.e., completes execution). For example, the latency of a simple instruction with no dependencies is \(1\).

Let \(|\alpha|\) denote the size of the formula \(\alpha\). It is defined as:

  • \(\;|p| = 0\), where \(p\) is an atomic proposition.
  • \(\;| eg \alpha| = 1 + |\alpha|\)
  • \(\;|\alpha \lor eta| = 1 + |\alpha| + | eta|\)

Let \(\mathrm{sf}(\alpha)\) denote the set of subformulas of the formula \(\alpha\). It is defined as:

  • \(\;\mathrm{sf}(p) = \{p\}\), where \(p\) is an atomic proposition.
  • \(\;\mathrm{sf}( eg \alpha) = \{( eg \alpha)\} \cup \mathrm{sf}(\alpha)\)
  • \(\;\mathrm{sf}((\alpha \lor eta)) = \{(\alpha \lor eta)\} \cup \mathrm{sf}(\alpha) \cup \mathrm{sf}( eta)\)

Let \(\#(\mathrm{sf}(\alpha))\) denote the number of subformulas of \(\alpha\).

Which of the following is/are true?

options.html: For every <span>\(i > 0\)</span>, there is at least one formula <span>\(\alpha_i\)</span> with <span>\(|\alpha_i| = i\)</span> and <span>\(\#(\mathrm{sf}(\alpha_i)) = 2|\alpha_i| + 1\)</span>
For every <span>\(i > 0\)</span>, there is at least one formula <span>\(\beta_i\)</span> with <span>\(|\beta_i| = i\)</span> and <span>\(\#(\mathrm{sf}(\beta_i)) < 2|\beta_i| + 1\)</span>

A leaky bucket traffic shaper has a leak rate of \(5\) packets/sec and a bucket size of \(20\) packets. The bucket is empty at \(t = 0\). Packets arriving when the bucket is full are dropped. After arrivals stop, the bucket continues leaking until it becomes empty.

The packet arrival rates are:

\[ \begin{array}{|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Start (sec)} & \text{End (sec)} & \text{Arrival rate (pkts/sec)} \\ \hline 0 & 4 & 6 \\ 4 & 7 & 10 \\ 7 & 9 & 8 \\ 9 & 12 & 4 \\ \hline \end{array} \]

In the table, the first row means that during the time interval from \(t = 0\) to \(t = 4\) seconds, packets arrive continuously at a rate of \(6\) packets per second.

Which option correctly gives the total time (from \(t = 0\)) for all packets to be transmitted and the total number of packets dropped?
questions.solution:

questions.html:
Sender A transmits packets to intermediate node B using Go-Back-\(N\) with a window size of \(3\). Packets are indexed starting from \(0\). On the A–B link, packet $1 ~(\mathrm{pkt1})$ and packet $4 ~(\mathrm{pkt4})$ are lost during their first transmission.

Node B forwards packets to receiver C using Selective Repeat with a window size of \(4\). When B finally receives $\mathrm{pkt4}$ from A and forwards it to C for the first time, $\mathrm{pkt4}$ arrives at C in error, so C does not acknowledge it.

Which packets must B have sent to C after the first transmission of $\mathrm{pkt4}$ and before the timeout caused by $\mathrm{pkt4}$?

A. None
B. \( \{\text{pkt5}\} \) only
C. \( \{\text{pkt5},\, \text{pkt6}\} \)
D. \( \{\text{pkt6}\} \) only
questions.solution:

Consider a system with three resource types \(A, B, C\) and four threads \(T1, T2, T3, T4\). The system is currently in the following state.

The total number of resources in the system is \( (A,B,C) = (12,9,12). \)

Current allocation \[ \begin{array}{c \quad c \quad c \quad c} \hline \text{Thread} & A & B & C \\ \hline T1 & 2 & 1 & 3 \\ T2 & 1 & 2 & 3 \\ T3 & 5 & 4 & 3 \\ T4 & 2 & 1 & 2 \\ \hline \end{array} \]
Maximum requirement \[ \begin{array}{c \quad c \quad c \quad c} \hline \text{Thread} & A & B & C \\ \hline T1 & 4 & 9 & 4 \\ T2 & 5 & 3 & 3 \\ T3 & 6 & 4 & 3 \\ T4 & 4 & 8 & 2 \\ \hline \end{array} \]

Let \((x,y,z)\) be the maximum number of additional copies of resources \((A,B,C)\) that thread \(T1\) can be granted in a single request without risking deadlock.

questions.html:
Consider the following modified version of Peterson’s algorithm. The variable turn is a shared variable accessible to both processes. Before entering the critical region, Process \(0\) calls enter(0,1) and Process \(1\) calls enter(1,0). Both \( \text{interest}[0] \) and \( \text{interest}[1] \) are initially \(0\).

void enter(int self, int other) {
    turn = other;              // turn is a shared variable
    interest[self] = 1;
    while (interest[other] == 1 && turn == other);
}

void leave(int self) {
    interest[self] = 0;
}

The above differs from the original Peterson's algorithm because \( \text{turn} \) is assigned before \( \text{interest[self]} \).

Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.html: The algorithm violates mutual exclusion for some interleavings.
The algorithm causes deadlock but mutual exclusion holds.
The algorithm is starvation-free but not deadlock-free.

questions.solution:
Answer: B

questions.html:
Consider the following concurrent program:

int slot = -1;
int array[2] = {0, 0};

function1() {
    P(m);
    slot++;
    V(m);

    int tid = get_counter();

    P(m);
    array[slot] = tid;
    V(m);
}
  • \(m\) is a binary semaphore initialized to \(1\).
  • slot and array are shared variables.
  • Two threads \(T_1\) and \(T_2\) execute function1().
  • get_counter() returns \(1\) for \(T_1\) and \(2\) for \(T_2\).

After both threads finish, which of the following can be the final contents of array?

Select all correct options.
questions.solution:
Answer: A, B, C, D

Consider the following C program:

typedef struct {
    int x, y;
} Point;

Point* add(Point* a, Point* b) {
    Point res;
    res.x = a->x + b->x;
    res.y = a->y + b->y;
    return &res;
}

int main() {
    Point a = {1, 2};

    Point* b;
    b->x = 3;
    b->y = 5;

    Point* c = malloc(sizeof(Point));
    c = add(&a, b);

    free(b);
    free(c);
}

Which of the following statements is/are correct?
